facts.text: Cardiogenic shock.
Sick sinus syndrome, second‑ or third‑degree atrioventricular block, or bradycardia leading to syncope in patients without a functioning pacemaker.
facts.population: Patients with conduction system disease lacking a pacemaker

facts.text: Known hypersensitivity to amiodarone, its components, or iodine.

Boxed warning: Amiodarone can cause life‑threatening pulmonary toxicity (incidence up to 17 %, fatal in ~10 %), hepatic injury (may be fatal), and pro‑arrhythmic effects. Baseline chest X‑ray, pulmonary function tests, and liver transaminases are required before initiation; repeat monitoring is recommended every 3–6 months.
Pulmonary toxicity may present as cough, dyspnea, interstitial/alveolar pneumonitis, or ARDS; consider prednisone 40–60 mg/day tapered if toxicity occurs.
Hepatic injury may be asymptomatic enzyme elevation or severe hepatitis/cirrhosis; discontinue or reduce dose if transaminases exceed 3 × ULN (or double a previously elevated baseline).

Amiodarone can exacerbate existing arrhythmias or precipitate new ventricular tachyarrhythmias, torsades de pointes, especially with electrolyte disturbances (K⁺, Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺). Correct electrolytes before initiation.
Corneal microdeposits are common and reversible; optic neuropathy/neuritis are rare but may cause permanent vision loss. Perform baseline and periodic ophthalmic examinations.

Thyroid dysfunction occurs in up to 10 % (hypothyroidism) and ~2 % (hyperthyroidism). Monitor thyroid function before and during therapy, especially in the elderly or those with prior thyroid disease.

Symptomatic bradycardia or sinus arrest may occur in 2–4 % of patients; may require pacemaker. Risk increased with concomitant negative chronotropes or antiviral therapy (e.g., ledipasvir/sofosbuvir).
Implantable cardioverter‑defibrillators or pacemakers may have altered pacing/defibrillation thresholds; assess thresholds at initiation and during therapy.
Fetal toxicity: amiodarone may cause cardiac, thyroid, neurodevelopmental, and growth effects in the neonate. Avoid use in pregnancy unless benefits outweigh risks.
Peripheral neuropathy may be irreversible after chronic use.
Photosensitivity occurs in ~10 % of patients; advise sun protection. Chronic therapy may cause blue‑gray skin discoloration.
Increased sensitivity to myocardial depressant and conduction effects of halogenated inhalational anesthetics; monitor closely during surgery.
Loading dose: 800–1600 mg/day (usually divided) until therapeutic response (1–3 weeks).
After response, reduce to 600–800 mg/day for one month, then maintain at ~400 mg/day.
Administer tablets with meals; for total daily doses ≥1000 mg or if GI intolerance occurs, give in divided doses with food.

Obtain baseline chest X‑ray, pulmonary function tests, thyroid function tests, and liver aminotransferases before starting therapy; correct hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, and hypocalcemia before initiation.
Patients >65 years have reduced clearance and prolonged half‑life; start at the low end of the dosing range and adjust for hepatic, renal, or cardiac impairment.
Monitor renal function when amiodarone is co‑administered with cyclosporine, as amiodarone can increase creatinine despite dose reduction of cyclosporine.

Pharmacodynamic: Concomitant QT‑prolonging drugs (class I/III antiarrhythmics, lithium, phenothiazines, tricyclic antidepressants, certain fluoroquinolones, macrolides, azole antifungals, halogenated anesthetics) increase torsades de pointes risk; avoid combination.
Negative chronotropes (digoxin, β‑blockers, verapamil, diltiazem, clonidine, ivabradine) potentiate bradycardia, sinus arrest, and AV block; monitor heart rate.
CYP450 inhibitors (grapefruit juice, certain fluoroquinolones/macrolides, azole antifungals, cimetidine, protease inhibitors) increase amiodarone exposure; avoid or adjust dose.
CYP450 inducers (St. John’s Wort) reduce amiodarone serum levels; may require dose increase.
Cyclosporine: amiodarone raises cyclosporine levels and may increase serum creatinine; monitor cyclosporine concentrations and renal function; consider dose reduction of cyclosporine.
Digoxin: amiodarone can double digoxin concentrations; reduce digoxin dose by ~50 % and monitor for toxicity.
Warfarin: amiodarone potentiates anticoagulant effect, increasing PT/INR up to 100 % after 3–4 days; reduce warfarin dose by 1/3–1/2 and monitor INR.
Statins (simvastatin, lovastatin, atorvastatin): increased plasma concentrations; limit lovastatin to ≤40 mg, simvastatin to ≤20 mg, consider lower starting doses of other CYP3A4 substrates.

Antiarrhythmics (quinidine, procainamide, flecainide): amiodarone inhibits their metabolism; start at 30‑50 % lower dose and monitor; reduce dose of the other agent for several days after switching to amiodarone.
Sofosbuvir (and ledipasvir/sofosbuvir): reports of severe bradyarrhythmia requiring pacemaker when started in patients on amiodarone; monitor heart rate and consider discontinuing amiodarone.
Lidocaine: may cause sinus bradycardia when combined with amiodarone; consider lower lidocaine dose and monitor heart rate.
Fentanyl: combination may cause hypotension, bradycardia, and decreased cardiac output; avoid co‑administration.
Cholestyramine: reduces amiodarone serum levels; may require dose adjustment.
Phenytoin: amiodarone increases steady‑state phenytoin levels; monitor phenytoin concentrations.
